prediction:
THOUGHT: A 5-year-old with marked upper-extremity hypertension is unusual and strongly suggests a secondary cause. Key physical findings—weak/trace femoral pulses compared with normal radial pulses and a systolic ejection murmur best heard along the left sternal border radiating to the back—point to an obstructive lesion of the aorta. The echocardiogram specifically shows narrowing of the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery with a pressure gradient, which is the classic location for congenital coarctation (usually just distal to the ligamentum arteriosum). The blood-pressure differential (high arms, lower legs) and diminished femoral pulses are explained by this obstruction. Chest x‑ray may show rib notching from collateral vessels in older children, but its absence in a young child is expected. Other secondary causes of pediatric hypertension (renal disease, endocrine causes) are less likely given the localizing cardiovascular exam and echo confirmation of a discrete aortic narrowing.  
DIAGNOSIS: Coarctation of the aorta (postductal coarctation distal to the left subclavian artery).
